questions.q:
The Class 7 farm club's record shows that the school hens laid 5, 6, 4, 6, 5 and 7 eggs on six days. Read the three statements.
Statement 1: 'On half of these days the hens laid 6 or more eggs' is a statistical statement.
Statement 2: 'The hens will probably lay about 5 or 6 eggs tomorrow' is a statistical statement.
Statement 3: 'The hens laid 7 eggs on the sixth day' is a summary of the whole record.
Which of the statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. The values 6, 6 and 7 are 3 of the 6 days, so Statement 1 summarises the record as a proportion. Statement 2 is a prediction drawn from the record, which also makes it a statistical statement. Statement 3 only repeats one value of the record, so it does not summarise the whole record.

questions.q: A class monitor's note says: 'Most students of Class 7B finish their tiffin in 20 to 30 minutes, and a few take more than 40 minutes.' (a) Write the statistical question that this note answers. (b) Say what data the monitor must have collected, and from whom. (c) Explain why the question 'How long did Farhan take to finish his tiffin today?' could not have led to this note.
questions.a: (a) For example: 'How long do the students of Class 7B take to finish their tiffin?' (b) The time taken by each student of Class 7B (or by many of them), collected on one or more days. (c) Farhan's question has one fixed answer about one person on one day. It gives a single value, and the words 'most' and 'a few' need many values that vary.
s: (a) writes a question about the time taken by the students of Class 7B as a group, whose answers vary
(b) names the data: tiffin times collected from the students of Class 7B
(c) explains that Farhan's question gives one value about one person, while 'most' and 'a few' need many varying values

questions.q: Mita asks, 'Typically, are erasers costlier at the school gate shop or at the market shop?' She visits both shops once, finds Rs 6 at the gate shop and Rs 5 at the market shop, and says, 'My question is a statistical question, and my visit has answered it: the gate shop is costlier.' Is Mita fully right, partly right or wrong? Explain, and say what she should do next.
questions.a: Partly right. Her question is a statistical question, because the word 'typically' asks about prices that can vary with time and with the kind of eraser, so data is needed. But one visit gives only one price from each shop, which is not enough to say what is typical; the gate shop was costlier on that one day only. She should note the prices at both shops on many days and then compare them, for example by their averages.
s: says the first part is right: it is a statistical question because prices can vary and data is needed
says the second part is wrong: one price from each shop cannot show what is typical
says she should collect prices on many days from both shops and compare them

questions.q: The Class 7 water monitors read the meter of the drinking-water tank on six school days. The litres used were 38, 42, 40, 44, 36 and 40. (a) Write one statistical question that this record can help to answer, and one question about the school's water that it cannot answer. (b) Find the mean and write a statistical statement that uses it. (c) Write a statistical statement in the form of a proportion, using the number of days on which at least the mean was used. (d) Write a statistical statement that is a prediction for the next school day. (e) The tank holds 45 litres and is filled once each morning. A monitor says, 'It is certain that the tank will never run out.' Is that a fair statement from this record? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Can answer: 'How much water is used on a school day?' Cannot answer, for example: 'Which class drinks the most water?', because the record has no class-wise values. (b) Total = 240 litres, mean = 240 / 6 = 40 litres, so 'On average 40 litres were used per day.' (c) 40, 42, 40 and 44 are at least 40, which is 4 of 6 days, so 'On two-thirds of these days at least 40 litres were used.' (d) For example: 'About 40 litres will probably be used on the next school day.' (e) Not fair. The highest use, 44 litres, is below 45, so the tank will probably be enough, but six days of data can only support 'probably', not 'never'; a hotter day could use more.
s: (a) writes one question the record can answer and one it cannot, with the missing data named or clear
(b) finds total 240 and mean 40 litres and writes a statement using it
(c) counts 4 of 6 days at or above 40 and writes it as a proportion
(d) writes a prediction for the next day that is close to the data and uses a word such as 'about' or 'probably'
(e) says not fair: 44 is below 45 so running out is unlikely, but six days support only a likely statement, not a certain one

questions.q: Twelve Class 7 students stand in one line, toe to heel, in their bare feet. The line is 2.76 m long. A rope of that length is folded into 12 equal parts. What does one part of the rope tell the class?
o: It is 23 cm, the mean foot length, even if no student's foot is exactly 23 cm
It is 23 cm, so every student in the line has a foot exactly 23 cm long
It is 2.3 cm, which is each student's equal share of the line
It is 23 cm, the median foot length, because the parts of the rope are equal
questions.a: It is 23 cm, the mean foot length, even if no student's foot is exactly 23 cm. 2.76 m = 276 cm, and 276 / 12 = 23 cm. The line is the total of the 12 foot lengths, so dividing it equally gives their mean; the mean says nothing about any one student's foot.

questions.q: Six rice sacks in the school kitchen weigh 52, 47, 53, 49, 51 and 54 kg. The cook wants the mean without adding the six weights. (a) Write how many kg each sack is above or below 50 kg. (b) Level these differences out to find the mean weight.
questions.a: (a) +2, -3, +3, -1, +1, +4. (b) Above 50 there are 2 + 3 + 1 + 4 = 10 kg and below 50 there are 3 + 1 = 4 kg, so 6 kg extra is left. Shared among 6 sacks this is 1 kg each, so the mean = 50 + 1 = 51 kg (check: 306 / 6 = 51).
s: (a) writes the differences +2, -3, +3, -1, +1, +4 from 50
(b) finds 6 kg extra overall, shares it among 6 sacks and gets mean 51 kg

questions.q: The garden club weighs 4 pumpkins at 5.2, 6.1, 4.9 and 5.8 kg, and 5 brinjals at 0.24, 0.31, 0.27, 0.22 and 0.21 kg. Kiran says, 'All the pumpkins together weigh 22 kg and all the brinjals 1.25 kg, and 22 / 1.25 = 17.6, so a pumpkin is about 18 times as heavy as a brinjal.' (a) Find the mean weight of a pumpkin and of a brinjal. (b) About how many times as heavy is a pumpkin as a brinjal? (c) Explain the mistake in Kiran's method.
questions.a: (a) Pumpkin: 22 / 4 = 5.5 kg. Brinjal: 1.25 / 5 = 0.25 kg. (b) 5.5 / 0.25 = 22, so a pumpkin is about 22 times as heavy. (c) Kiran compared totals of groups of different sizes: there are 4 pumpkins but 5 brinjals, so his brinjal total includes one extra vegetable. The means remove the effect of group size.
s: (a) finds the means 5.5 kg and 0.25 kg
(b) divides the means and gets about 22 times
(c) says Kiran is wrong because totals of groups of different sizes cannot be compared this way

questions.q: Seven girls threaded 14, 18, 9, 12, 15, 10 and 13 beads for the art room. Before the count was finished, Gauri, who threaded 13, went home. Her friend Ila says, 'I do not need to add again. The mean of the other six is the same as the mean of all seven.' (a) Check Ila's statement with numbers. (b) Explain, using the idea of a fair share, why it had to happen. (c) Find the mean of the other six if instead the girl who threaded 9 had gone home, to two decimal places.
questions.a: (a) Ila is right. All seven: total 91, mean 91 / 7 = 13. The other six: 91 - 13 = 78, mean 78 / 6 = 13. (b) 13 is exactly the fair share, so Gauri takes away just her own share. Nothing has to be shared out again among the others. (c) (91 - 9) / 6 = 82 / 6 = 13.67 beads. The mean goes up because a girl below the fair share has left.
s: (a) finds 91 / 7 = 13 and 78 / 6 = 13 and says Ila is right
(b) explains that Gauri held exactly the fair share, so the share of the others does not change

questions.q: For the kite festival, Team Neem (5 members) made 6, 11, 4, 12 and 7 kites, and Team Peepal (4 members) made 9, 10, 5 and 8 kites. (a) Find the mean number of kites per member in each team. (b) Team Neem wants every member to hold the same number of kites. At least how many kites must change hands? (c) How many more kites must Team Peepal make so that its mean becomes 1 more than Team Neem's? (d) Team Banyan also has 5 members. Pia says, 'Banyan has as many members as Neem, so its mean must also be 8.' Say whether her statement must be true, and show this with two possible lists of kites for Team Banyan.
questions.a: (a) Neem: 40 / 5 = 8. Peepal: 32 / 4 = 8. (b) The members above 8 hold 3 + 4 = 7 extra kites, and the members below 8 need 2 + 4 + 1 = 7, so at least 7 kites must change hands. (c) A mean of 9 for 4 members needs 36 kites, so Peepal must make 36 - 32 = 4 more. (d) It need not be true. The number of members alone does not fix the total, so the mean cannot be known. For example, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8 has mean 8, but 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 has mean 7 (any two lists with different means will do).
s: (a) finds both means, 8 and 8
(b) finds that the extra above 8 is 7 kites, so 7 must change hands
(c) finds 4 x 9 = 36 and 36 - 32 = 4 more kites
(d) says it need not be true, because the same number of members does not mean the same total
(d) gives two lists of five values with different means, at least one different from 8

questions.q:
Two dot plots show the number of pencils in each student's pencil box. Class 7A: one dot at 2, three dots at 3, four dots at 4 and two dots at 5. Class 7B: two dots at 1, one dot at 2, two dots at 4, three dots at 5 and two dots at 8.
Statement 1: The difference between the highest and lowest values is 4 more for Class 7B than for Class 7A.
Statement 2: The plot of Class 7A shows that the third student on the register has 5 pencils.
Statement 3: More students of Class 7B than of Class 7A have 4 or more pencils.
Which of the statements are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Class 7A: 5 - 2 = 3 and Class 7B: 8 - 1 = 7, a gap of 4 more. A dot plot sorts the values and loses the original order, so it cannot say what any one student on the register has. With 4 or more pencils there are 4 + 2 = 6 students in Class 7A and 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 in Class 7B.

questions.q: Anu counted the paper boats she folded on 6 days, but the page got wet. She remembers only that the lowest count was 3, the highest was 11 and the mean was 7. (a) Find the total for the 6 days and the difference between the highest and lowest counts. (b) How many boats do the other 4 days add up to? (c) Write one possible full list of the 6 counts.
questions.a: (a) Total = 6 x 7 = 42 boats; difference = 11 - 3 = 8. (b) 42 - 3 - 11 = 28 boats. (c) For example 3, 6, 7, 7, 8, 11 (the four middle values must add to 28, and each must be from 3 to 11).
s: (a) finds the total 42 and the difference 8
(b) finds that the other four days add to 28
(c) gives six counts including 3 and 11, all from 3 to 11, with total 42

questions.q: The laps swum by two swim-club squads were: Squad X: 10, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 30. Squad Y: 10, 12, 15, 20, 25, 28, 30. Tanvi says, 'The lowest value, the highest value and the mean are the same for both squads, so their dot plots will look the same.' (a) Check the three values she names. (b) Describe how the dots of each squad would lie on a dot plot. (c) Is her conclusion right? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Both have lowest 10 and highest 30. Both totals are 140, so both means are 140 / 7 = 20. (b) Squad X: five dots stacked at 20, with one dot alone at each end. Squad Y: seven single dots spread evenly from 10 to 30. (c) No. The three values match, but they do not show how the data is clustered or spread between the ends; only the dot plot shows this, and the two plots look very different.
s: (a) confirms lowest 10, highest 30 and mean 20 for both squads
(b) describes X as clustered at 20 and Y as spread out from 10 to 30
(c) says her conclusion is wrong, because equal ends and means do not fix how the values are clustered

questions.q:
The Class 7 traffic squad counted the bicycles that came in through two school gates on 6 days.
Day | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
North gate | 52 | 48 | 61 | 47 | 58 | 52
South gate | 55 | 50 | 26 | 52 | 62 | 55
On Day 3 the South gate was half closed for repairs. Four students speak. Lata: 'South is busier, because it has the highest count.' Omar: 'North is busier, because its total is higher.' Sneha: 'South is busier, because it beats North on more days.' Vikram: 'North's counts stay closer together.' (a) Check Lata's fact and say why one value is weak evidence. (b) Check Omar's fact and find both means. (c) Check Sneha's fact. (d) Check Vikram's fact. (e) Which gate is busier on a usual day? Support your answer by leaving out Day 3.
questions.a: (a) True: the highest count is 62, at South. But it is one day only and says nothing about the other days. (b) True: North 318, South 300; means 318 / 6 = 53 and 300 / 6 = 50. (c) True: South is higher on Days 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, that is, 5 of 6 days. (d) True: the differences between highest and lowest are 61 - 47 = 14 for North and 62 - 26 = 36 for South. (e) South. Without Day 3 the means are (318 - 61) / 5 = 51.4 for North and (300 - 26) / 5 = 54.8 for South. North's higher total came only from the day South was half closed.
s: (a) confirms 62 at South and says one value does not describe the other days
(b) finds totals 318 and 300 and means 53 and 50
(c) finds South higher on 5 of the 6 days
(d) finds the differences 14 and 36, so Vikram is right
(e) chooses South, with means 51.4 and 54.8 without Day 3

questions.q: Two groups made paper bags in one hour. Group P: 38, 41, 42, 40 and 39 bags. Group Q: 12, 10, 14, 40 and 11 bags. What can be said about the value 40?
o: It is an outlier only in Group Q, as it lies far from the other values there
It is an outlier in both groups, as it is far above the median of Group Q
It is an outlier only in Group P, as it is the middle value there
It is an outlier in neither group, as it lies between 10 and 42
questions.a: It is an outlier only in Group Q, as it lies far from the other values there. In Group Q the others are 10 to 14, so 40 deviates a lot. In Group P the others are 38 to 42, so 40 sits among them. Being an outlier depends on the rest of the data, not on the size of the number.

questions.q: True or False: The median number of push-ups done by 10 cadets is reported as 17.5. Nobody can do half a push-up, so this median must be wrong. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. With 10 values, an even number, the median is the average of the two middle values. If they are 17 and 18, the median is (17 + 18) / 2 = 17.5. A median need not be a value in the data.
s: says False
explains that with an even count the median is the average of the two middle values, for example 17 and 18, so it need not be a value in the data

questions.q: The reading speeds (words per minute) of 12 students are 78, 92, 85, 101, 88, 110, 95, 83, 120, 90, 104 and 99. The teacher wants two equal groups, one below a certain speed and one above it. Anil says, 'Use the mean as the dividing speed.' (a) Find the mean to two decimal places, and count the students below and above it. (b) Find the median. (c) Is Anil's idea right? Give a reason using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Total = 1145, mean = 1145 / 12 = 95.42 words per minute. Below it: 78, 83, 85, 88, 90, 92, 95, which is 7 students; above it: 5 students. (b) Sorted: 78, 83, 85, 88, 90, 92, 95, 99, 101, 104, 110, 120. Median = (92 + 95) / 2 = 93.5. (c) No. The mean gives groups of 7 and 5. The median has an equal number of values on each side, so 93.5 gives 6 and 6.
s: (a) finds the mean 95.42 and counts 7 below and 5 above
(b) sorts the speeds and finds the median (92 + 95) / 2 = 93.5
(c) says Anil is wrong: the mean gives 7 and 5, while the median gives 6 and 6

questions.q: Nine students wear shoes of sizes 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7 and 8. The PT teacher wants one size such that exactly 4 students wear a smaller size and exactly 4 wear a bigger size. (a) Find the median size. (b) How many students wear a size smaller than the median, and how many a bigger size? (c) Show that no size can do what the teacher wants.
questions.a: (a) The fifth value of the sorted list is 5, so the median is 5. (b) 3 students wear smaller (3, 4, 4) and 3 wear bigger (6, 7, 8). (c) Three students wear size 5. Any size above 5 has at least 6 students below it. Size 5 has only 3 below, and any size below 5 has fewer than 3 below. So exactly 4 smaller is impossible, because the sizes jump from 3 students to 6 students.
s: (a) finds the median 5
(b) counts 3 smaller and 3 bigger
(c) shows that the three students of size 5 make the count below jump from 3 to 6, so exactly 4 is impossible

questions.q:
A science club noted the days that 8 bean seeds took to sprout: 9, 6, 7, 21, 8, 7, 6, 8. Renu wrote this working.
Line 1: The two middle numbers are 21 and 8, so the median is (21 + 8) / 2 = 14.5.
Line 2: Then I sorted the numbers. The two middle numbers are 7 and 8, so the median is 8, the bigger one.
Line 3: The outlier is 6, because it is the smallest number.
Line 4: The mean is 9, so the mean describes a typical seed better than the median.
(a) What is wrong with Line 1? (b) Correct Line 2. (c) Correct Line 3 and give a reason. (d) Find the mean with and without the outlier, to two decimal places where needed. (e) Is Line 4 right? Use the number of seeds that sprouted in fewer than 9 days.
questions.a: (a) She took the middle of the list as written. The data must be sorted first. (b) Sorted: 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 21. With 8 values the median is the average of the two middle values: (7 + 8) / 2 = 7.5 days. (c) The outlier is 21, because it lies far from the rest (6 to 9). The value 6 is the smallest but it is close to the others. (d) With 21: 72 / 8 = 9 days. Without 21: 51 / 7 = 7.29 days. (e) No. 6 of the 8 seeds took fewer than 9 days, so 9 is pulled up by the outlier. The median 7.5 describes a typical seed better.
s: (a) says the data was not sorted before the middle was taken
(b) gives the median (7 + 8) / 2 = 7.5 days
(c) names 21 as the outlier because it is far from the rest, and says 6 is close to the others
(d) finds the means 9 and 51 / 7 = 7.29 days
(e) says Line 4 is wrong: 6 of 8 seeds took fewer than 9 days, so the median represents better

questions.q: Seven students took 3, 28, 30, 31, 32, 34 and 58 minutes to finish a clay model. The student who took 3 minutes gave up early, and the one who took 58 minutes restarted. What is true of the mean and the median of all seven times?
o: They are close, as the two outliers pull the mean in opposite directions
The mean is far above the median, as 58 is an outlier at the higher end
The mean is far below the median, as 3 is an outlier at the lower end
They are equal, as an outlier never changes the mean of a list
questions.a: They are close, as the two outliers pull the mean in opposite directions. Total = 216, mean = 216 / 7 = 30.86 (about 30.9) minutes, and the median is 31 minutes. The low outlier and the high outlier nearly balance each other.

questions.q: The school first-aid room noted the students who came on 8 days: 6, 0, -, 9, 0, 3, -, 6. A 0 means the room was open and nobody came; a dash means the room was closed. (a) Find the correct mean and median per day. (b) A helper writes 0 for each dash and finds the mean and median again. Find her values. (c) Which of the two measures did her mistake change more, and why must the dashes be left out?
questions.a: (a) Six values: 0, 0, 3, 6, 6, 9. Total 24, mean 24 / 6 = 4. Median = (3 + 6) / 2 = 4.5. (b) Eight values: 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 6, 6, 9. Mean = 24 / 8 = 3. Median = (0 + 3) / 2 = 1.5. (c) The median changed more (by 3) than the mean (by 1), since the two extra zeros moved the middle of the sorted list. A dash is no value at all: the room was closed, so nothing was measured, while a 0 is a real count from an open day.
s: (a) uses six values and finds mean 4 and median 4.5
(b) uses eight values and finds mean 3 and median 1.5
(c) says the median changed more (3 against 1) and that a dash is not a value because the room was closed

questions.q: Seven students made seed balls for a tree-planting day. The counts were 34, 41, 45, 48, 52 and 57, and one more that is smudged, but the teacher remembers it was higher than 57. (a) Find the median, or explain why it cannot be found. (b) Can the exact mean be found? Give a reason. (c) Show that the mean must be more than 47.7.
questions.a: (a) It can be found. The smudged value is the largest, so the sorted list is 34, 41, 45, 48, 52, 57, then that value. The fourth value is the median: 48. (b) No. The mean needs the total of all seven values, and one of them is unknown. (c) The six known values add to 277. The seventh is more than 57, so the total is more than 334, and the mean is more than 334 / 7 = 47.71, which is more than 47.7.
s: (a) places the smudged value last and gets the median 48
(b) says the exact mean cannot be found because it needs the total of all the values
(c) uses 277 + 57 = 334 and 334 / 7 = 47.71 to show the mean is more than 47.7

questions.q: The school office noted the photocopy sheets used on 10 days: 120, 130, 125, 135, 130, 128, 132, 127, 133 and 640. The 640 was the day the exam papers were printed, and this happens once in every 10 school days. (a) Find the mean sheets per day. (b) Find the median sheets per day. (c) The office must buy paper for the next 20 school days. Work out the sheets needed if it plans with the mean and if it plans with the median, and say which plan is safe. (d) The office assistant asks how many sheets to keep near the machine on a usual day. Which measure should she use, and why? (e) Hari says, 'An outlier makes the mean useless, so we should never use it here.' Using (c) and (d), say whether he is right.
questions.a: (a) Total = 1800, mean = 1800 / 10 = 180 sheets. (b) Sorted, the two middle values are 130 and 130, so the median is 130 sheets. (c) Mean plan: 20 x 180 = 3600. Median plan: 20 x 130 = 2600. The 20 days include 2 exam days, so the real need is about 2 x 1800 = 3600. The mean plan is safe; the median plan falls about 1000 sheets short. (d) The median, 130: nine of the ten days lie between 120 and 135, and 180 is above all of them. (e) He is not right. The median is better for a usual day, but the mean is what gives the total, because the mean keeps the outlier in the sum. The choice depends on the question asked.
s: (a) finds the total 1800 and mean 180
(b) finds the median 130
(c) finds 3600 and 2600 and picks the mean plan because the 20 days include 2 exam days
(d) picks the median 130 because nine days lie from 120 to 135, all below 180
(e) says Hari is wrong: the mean is the right measure for finding a total, the median for a usual day

questions.q: A double bar graph shows the clay lamps made by Class 6 and Class 7 each week, with 1 unit = 12 lamps. In Week 3 the two bars placed end to end would measure 7.5 units, and the Class 6 bar is 1.5 units longer than the Class 7 bar. How many lamps did Class 6 make in Week 3?
o: 54 lamps
36 lamps
72 lamps
90 lamps
questions.a: 54 lamps. Removing the extra 1.5 units leaves 6 units, which is 3 units for each bar, so Class 7's bar is 3 units and Class 6's is 4.5 units. Class 6 made 4.5 x 12 = 54 lamps (Class 7 made 36, and the total is 90).

questions.q:
A double bar graph shows the saplings watered by two classes, with 1 unit = 6 saplings. Class 6 bars: Term 1 2.5 units, Term 2 4 units, Term 3 3.5 units. Class 8 bars: Term 1 3 units, Term 2 1.5 units, Term 3 5 units. Match each reading with its value.
Column I
1. Class 6's total for the three terms
2. Class 8's mean per term
3. The largest gap between the two classes in one term
4. Both classes together in Term 3
Column II
a. 19
b. 51
c. 60
d. 15
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b. Class 6 saplings are 15, 24 and 21, total 60. Class 8 saplings are 18, 9 and 30, total 57, mean 19. The gaps are 3, 15 and 9, so the largest is 15. Term 3 together is 21 + 30 = 51.

questions.q: The school's solar meter shows the units made by two roofs. Roof X: January 527, February 504. Roof Y: January 465, February 476. Zoya says, 'Roof X made less in February than in January in all, but on an average day it made more in February.' (a) Find Roof X's average units per day in each month, taking 31 days for January and 28 for February. (b) Is Zoya right? Say why a month's total can mislead here. (c) In a double bar graph of units per day with 1 unit = 2 units per day, how long is Roof Y's February bar?
questions.a: (a) January: 527 / 31 = 17 units per day. February: 504 / 28 = 18 units per day. (b) Yes, she is right. The total fell from 527 to 504, but the average per day rose from 17 to 18. February has fewer days, so its total can be smaller even though each day is better. (c) Roof Y's February average is 476 / 28 = 17 units per day, so the bar is 17 / 2 = 8.5 units long.
s: (a) finds 17 and 18 units per day for Roof X
(b) says Zoya is right because February has fewer days, so the total hides the higher daily average
(c) finds 476 / 28 = 17 and the bar length 8.5 units

questions.q:
Twenty students each of Class 6 and Class 8 chose a club: d = drama, m = music, s = science, n = none.
Class 6: d m s d n d m d s m d n d s m d d n m d
Class 8: s s m d s n s m s d s n s m s d s s m n
(a) Count the students who chose each option in each class. (b) The graph paper is 6 units tall. Give a whole-number scale for a double bar graph that fits, and show that it fits. (c) Using your scale, give the two bar lengths for the club with the largest gap between the classes.
questions.a: (a) Class 6: drama 9, music 5, science 3, none 3. Class 8: drama 3, music 4, science 10, none 3. (b) The tallest bar is 10. With 1 unit = 2 students it is 5 units, which fits in 6 units. (Any whole-number scale of 2 or more students fits.) (c) The gaps are 6 for drama, 1 for music, 7 for science and 0 for none, so science has the largest. With 1 unit = 2 students the bars are 3 / 2 = 1.5 units and 10 / 2 = 5 units.
s: (a) gives all eight counts correctly
(b) gives a whole-number scale of 2 or more and shows that the bar for 10 fits in 6 units
(c) picks science, the gap of 7, and gives its two bar lengths for that scale

questions.q:
Class 7 estimated and then measured five objects, in cm.
Object | Estimate | Measure
Water bottle | 25 | 22
Tiffin box | 18 | 20
Library book | 30 | 28
Pencil pouch | 16 | 13
Lunch mat | 24 | 26
They will draw a double bar graph on a page 7 units tall. (a) Show that 1 unit = 4 cm does not fit but 1 unit = 5 cm does. (b) With 1 unit = 5 cm, find the two bar lengths for the pencil pouch. (c) For which objects will the Estimate bar be shorter than the Measure bar, and what does this tell us about those estimates? (d) Find the average positive difference between the estimates and the measures. (e) Riya subtracts Measure from Estimate for each object, keeping the signs, and says, 'The average is only 0.8 cm.' Show how she got this, and explain why it makes the class look better than it was.
questions.a: (a) The tallest bar is 30 cm. 30 / 4 = 7.5 units is more than 7, but 30 / 5 = 6 units fits. (b) Estimate 16 / 5 = 3.2 units, Measure 13 / 5 = 2.6 units. (c) Tiffin box and lunch mat; the class underestimated these two. (d) Positive differences 3, 2, 2, 3, 2: total 12, average 12 / 5 = 2.4 cm. (e) Riya has +3, -2, +2, +3, -2, which adds to 4, and 4 / 5 = 0.8. The overestimates and the underestimates cancel each other, so the 0.8 hides that the class was really off by 2.4 cm per object on average.
s: (a) shows 30 / 4 = 7.5 is over 7 and 30 / 5 = 6 fits
(b) finds 3.2 units and 2.6 units
(c) names the tiffin box and the lunch mat as underestimated
(d) finds the positive differences and the average 2.4 cm
(e) shows +3, -2, +2, +3, -2 total 4 and 4 / 5 = 0.8, and explains that overestimates and underestimates cancel

questions.q: A school's record gives the saplings planted by its nine sections: 52, 44, 41, 30, 30, 27, 19, 16 and 12. Section 7C planted one of the two 30s. Which statement can be justified from this record?
o: Only 3 sections planted more than 7C, and only 4 planted fewer
Only 3 sections planted more than 7C, and only 5 planted fewer
Only 4 sections planted more than 7C, and only 4 planted fewer
The top section planted more than twice as many as 7C
questions.a: Only 3 sections planted more than 7C, and only 4 planted fewer. 52, 44 and 41 are more; 27, 19, 16 and 12 are fewer. The other 30 is neither more nor fewer, so the two counts add to 7, not 8. The top section's 52 is less than 2 x 30 = 60.

questions.q:
True or False: The table is a school's record of the average number of library books borrowed per student in a year. The table justifies the statement 'In each of these years, Class 7 borrowed more on average than Class 6.' Give the verdict and a reason.
Class | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025
5 | 12.6 | 14.2 | 15.1 | 16.4
6 | 13.0 | 16.5 | 17.2 | 18.9
7 | 13.8 | 18.1 | 19.6 | 19.2
8 | 10.5 | 12.4 | 13.0 | 16.1
questions.a: True. Class 7 against Class 6: 13.8 > 13.0, 18.1 > 16.5, 19.6 > 17.2 and 19.2 > 18.9, so Class 7's average is higher in all four years, though the gap is only 0.3 in 2025.
s: says True
gives the four comparisons 13.8 > 13.0, 18.1 > 16.5, 19.6 > 17.2 and 19.2 > 18.9

questions.q:
The table is a school's record of the average number of library books borrowed per student in a year. Students move up one class each year.
Class | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025
5 | 12.6 | 14.2 | 15.1 | 16.4
6 | 13.0 | 16.5 | 17.2 | 18.9
7 | 13.8 | 18.1 | 19.6 | 19.2
8 | 10.5 | 12.4 | 13.0 | 16.1
Asha is in Class 7 in 2025. She says, 'The Class 7 row rose by 5.4 books from 2022 to 2025, so my own batch has raised its average by 5.4 books since 2022.' (a) Check the number 5.4. (b) Whose averages does the Class 7 row show? (c) Which values of the table follow Asha's batch? Find the rise from the earliest of these values to 2025.
questions.a: Asha is partly right: her number is right but it does not describe her batch. (a) 19.2 - 13.8 = 5.4, so the number is right. (b) The row shows a different set of children each year, namely whoever was in Class 7 in that year. (c) Her batch was in Class 6 in 2024 (17.2) and in Class 5 in 2023 (14.2), and the table has no value for them in 2022. Rise from 2023 to 2025 = 19.2 - 14.2 = 5.0 books.
s: (b) says the row shows different children each year, so it does not follow her batch
(c) follows the batch through 14.2, 17.2 and 19.2 and finds the rise 5.0

questions.q:
A school's record of its students' heights (cm) is below.
Class | Lowest | Mean | Highest
6 | 124 | 140 | 162
7 | 128 | 146 | 170
8 | 133 | 152 | 178
A new laboratory will be used by Classes 6 to 8. (a) Ravi wants the height of the door to be the mean of the three class means. Find this height, find how many cm it is below the tallest student, and say which number in the table the door should be planned from. Decide whether the table justifies each statement, with a reason. (b) 'Every Class 8 student is taller than every Class 6 student.' (c) 'At least one Class 6 student is taller than at least one Class 8 student.' (d) 'Half of the Class 7 students are taller than 146 cm.' (e) 'Of the three classes, Class 8 has the largest gap between its shortest and tallest students.'
questions.a: (a) (140 + 146 + 152) / 3 = 146 cm, which is 178 - 146 = 32 cm below the tallest student. The door must let everyone pass, so it should be planned from the highest value, 178 cm, not from a mean. (b) Not justified: the tallest in Class 6 is 162 cm and the shortest in Class 8 is 133 cm. (c) Justified, by the same two numbers: 162 > 133. (d) Not justified: 146 is the mean, not the median, and only the median has half the values above it. (e) Justified: the gaps are 38, 42 and 45 cm.
s: (a) finds 146 cm and 32 cm, and says the door must be planned from the highest value 178 cm
(b) says not justified, using 162 > 133
(c) says justified, using 162 > 133
(d) says not justified because 146 is a mean, not a median
(e) says justified, with the gaps 38, 42 and 45 cm
